{"rule":"Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and, in the text field, the passage of about 250 words that comes immediately AFTER the current text in the same story.","text":"Mara let go of the handle. The tune stopped at once.

“That’s our song,” Tomas whispered. “But who’s playing it?”

The shepherd tilted his head. “Someone who remembers.”

He opened the door.

Beyond it was a round chamber with a ceiling lost in darkness. A single lantern burned on a stone table. Beside it sat a woman in a gray coat, her silver hair braided with tiny bells. She looked up as they entered, and the shepherd’s flute slipped from his hands.

“Grandmother?” he said.

The woman rose. For a heartbeat, she seemed ready to embrace him. Then she glanced at the bells on the walls, and sorrow crossed her face.

“I’m not your grandmother,” she said gently. “Not anymore.”

Mara looked from one to the other. “What does that mean?”

The woman lifted a small brass bell from the table. Its clapper was missing. “Long ago, the hill kept every sound that was lost. A name forgotten. A promise broken. A note that never found its way home.” She turned the bell in her palm. “Your shepherd came here seeking one of those sounds.”

The shepherd stared at the floor. “I came to bring you back.”

“And I came back,” she said. “But the hill has kept something in return.”

A faint hum shivered through the chamber. On the door behind them, the brass plate began to glow. The engraved bell had changed: now it showed a tiny figure standing beside an open gate.

Mara’s book grew warm beneath her arm. She opened it, and a fresh line appeared:

To leave with what you love, give the hill what it has never heard.

Tomas swallowed. “And what’s that?”

The woman looked at their instruments.

“A song,” she said, “that belongs to no one alone.”"}
